newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian hospital group branches out.
newsitem.headline: Indian hospital group branches out.

text.p: India's Apollo Hospitals Group, following the success of its pioneering ventures across the country, is taking its expertise overseas, its chairman said on Monday.
Dr Prathap C. Reddy, chairman and founder of Apollo Hospitals Group, told Reuters the group was setting up hospitals in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Oman.
Apollo hospitals already draw patients from overseas, with the bulk coming from neighbouring countries, for treatment unavailable or too expensive at home.
Reddy said a 150-bed hospital in Nepal was commissioned in the last quarter of 1996 at a cost of $8.5 million.
The cardiologist and entrepreneur said there were plans to set up hospitals in Africa and East Europe.
Apollo institutions have earned a reputation in heart surgery and in the treatment of kidney ailments, among other specialised areas.

Apollo, which opened its first hospital in 1983 in the southern city of Madras where the group has its headquarters, has 13 hospitals and specialised healthcare centres in India with 2,090 beds. There are 10 more centres with 2,050 beds under construction or on the drawing board.
Hospital projects abroad are in Dhaka (500 beds at $40 million cost), Colombo (300 beds at $28.5 million) and Muscat (100 beds at $18 million). These are due for completion between 1997 and 1999.
Reddy said profit was not the group's motivating force. "We (India) are the best among developing nations in terms of professional skills, manpower, managerial talents and cost-effective services."

The death of a friend from a heart ailment spurred Reddy to set up his first facility in Madras. "I had worked in the United States for 11 years and returned in 1982. Then a friend died for lack of proper treatment. It should never have happened."
The Apollo Group is also involved in pharmacy outlets, medical equipment leasing, financing, health insurance and managed care.
The group said it had completed 20,000 operations in cardiac surgery with a 98 percent success rate.
Reddy lamented the failure of India's government to give the industry its due, despite the progress made in raising standards.
"We need to be treated as an infrastructure industry. Healthcare should be treated on par with other core industries."

Reddy said the group was seeking concessions, such as zero import duties on medical equipment, tax holidays and equal treatment for hospitals and hotels, which pay lower rates for power, water and other amenities.
"If these concessions are given, the healthcare sector will attract the largest amount of foreign investment," he said.
